ety.text: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw Proto-Italic *oktō Latin octō Latin Octōberlbor. Old French octobrebor. Middle English [Term?] English Octoberbor. Classical Persian اَکْتُوبَر (aktūbar)bor.? Hindi अक्टूबर Borrowed from Portuguese outubro, influenced by English October. Compare Classical Persian اَکْتُوبَر (aktūbar), Konkani ओतुब्र (otubra), Marathi आक्तोबर (āktobar), all of which could be possible intermediaries.
From Sanskrit अगरु (agaru). Ultimately from Tamil அகில் (akil, “eagle-wood”).

ety.text: Etymology tree Sanskrit अङ्ग् (aṅg) Proto-Indo-European *-nósder. Sanskrit -अन (-ana) Sanskrit अङ्गन (aṅgana) Prakrit 𑀅𑀁𑀕𑀡 (aṃgaṇa) Hindi आँगन Inherited from Prakrit 𑀅𑀁𑀕𑀡 (aṃgaṇa), from Sanskrit अङ्गन (aṅgana), from अङ्ग् (aṅg) + -अन (-ana). Doublet of अंगन (aṅgan). Cognate with Maithili आङन (āṅan) / 𑒂𑒓𑒢 (āṅana), Sindhi اَڱَڻُ (aṅaṇu) / अङणु, Gujarati આંગણ (ā̃gaṇ), Marathi अंगण (aṅgaṇ), Konkani आंगण (āṅgaṇ).
Borrowed from Classical Persian عِزَّت (izzat), from Arabic عِزَّة (ʕizza). Compare Assamese ইজ্জত (izzot), Bengali ইজ্জত (ijjot), Punjabi ਇੱਜ਼ਤ (izzat).

s.g: the sitting of a court of justice

ety.text: Inherited from Sanskrit कटकटा (kaṭakaṭā, “sound of rubbing”), ultimately onomatopoeic; a reduplication. Related to कड़कना (kaṛaknā).

ety.text: Borrowed from Konkani कोंकणी (koṅkṇī). By surface analysis, कोंकण (kõkaṇ) + -ई (-ī).
Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀓𑁄𑀠 (koḍha), from Sanskrit कुष्ठ (kúṣṭha).

Inherited from Prakrit गिद्ध (giddha). Doublet of गिद्ध (giddh) and गृध्र (gŕdhra, “vulturine, rapacious”). In the sense of "dodo", based on the similar bald head and long neck, annotated in a painting between 1624-5 by Ustad Mansur.
Borrowed from Classical Persian گمان (gumān). Doublet of विमन (viman, “sad, disconsolate”), a tatsama from Sanskrit विमनस् (vimanas, “sad, disconsolate”).

s.g: confusion or mess created with an ill-intention: deception, plot, scam, fraud

ety.text: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-der.? Sanskrit घन (ghana) Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ Sanskrit -ता (-tā) Sanskrit घनता (ghanatā)bor. Hindi घनता Borrowed from Sanskrit घनता (ghanatā). By surface analysis, घन (ghan, “dense”) + -ता (-tā, “-ity”). In the physics sense, semantic loan from English density.
Borrowed from Classical Persian ظاهر (zāhir), from Arabic ظَاهِر (ẓāhir).

ety.text: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr Proto-Indo-Iranian *máHtā Sanskrit मातृ (mātṛ)lbor. Hindi माता Learned borrowing from Sanskrit माता (mātā), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *máHtā, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Doublet of माँ (mā̃). In the sense of "smallpox" and "chickenpox," compare other-language epithets for the goddess Shitala and words for "mother" or "goddess" like Sanskrit शीतला (śītalā, “Shitala, smallpox”), Assamese আই (ai, “mother, smallpox”), Marathi देवी (devī, “goddess, smallpox”), and Tamil அம்மை (ammai, “mother, smallpox”).
Inherited from Sanskrit मत्तक (mattaka, “intoxicated”). See also माँत (mā̃t).
Borrowed from Classical Persian روزگار (rōzgār, “time, period”). Compare Bengali রোজগার (rōjogar), Punjabi ਰੁਜ਼ਗਾਰ (ruzgār).

s.g: to be embarrassed, to feel ashamed

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian حِنَا (hinā), a variant of حِنَّا (hinnā), حِنَّاء (hinnā'), from Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ). Cognate with English henna, Spanish alheña, Punjabi ਹਿਨਾ (hinā), and Bengali হেনা (hena).
